bib.title: OctoPack: Instruction Tuning Code Large Language Models

read.skipped: Reference list and the Table 4 per-language numeric rows skimmed only; Appendix R model-output example listings (Figures 26-39) not read line by line.

question: Can Git commits (code change plus commit message) serve as permissively licensed instruction data that improves instruction-tuned Code LLMs, without using OpenAI-generated outputs?
hypothesis: Including many programming languages in instruction tuning boosts performance further, and code data (commits) should behave the same way as natural-language instruction data.
contributions: COMMITPACK and COMMITPACKFT: 4TB of permissively licensed code commits across 350 programming languages for pretraining and a filtered 2GB variant containing high-quality code instructions used for finetuning
HUMANEVALPACK: A benchmark for Code LLM generalization, spanning three scenarios (Code Repair, Code Explanation, Code Synthesis) and 6 programming languages (Python, JavaScript, Java, Go, C++, Rust)
OCTOCODER and OCTOGEEX: The best permissive Code LLMs

method.summary: Builds COMMITPACK (4TB of single-file GitHub commits, 350 languages) and a heavily filtered 2GB subset COMMITPACKFT (277 languages, commit message as instruction). Instruction-tunes StarCoder 16B (LoRA) on 5,000 random COMMITPACKFT samples plus filtered OASST to get OctoCoder, ablates against xP3x, Self-Instruct and OASST, and evaluates on HumanEvalPack (new human-written 6-language, 3-task extension of HumanEval).
method.task: instruction tuning of code LLMs; evaluation on code repair, code explanation, code synthesis

datasets.name: COMMITPACK
datasets.source: GitHub Archive (GH Archive) metadata on Google BigQuery, commits up to 2016, plus scraped before/after files; licences MIT, Artistic-2.0, ISC, CC0-1.0, EPL-1.0, MPL-2.0, Apache-2.0, BSD-3-Clause, AGPL-3.0, LGPL-2.1, BSD-2-Clause or none
datasets.preprocessing: Table 5: commit message 5-10,000 chars, noise messages removed, single-file commits only, opt-out users removed

datasets.name: COMMITPACKFT
datasets.size: ~2GB; 742,273 samples; 277 languages (Table 1); 702,062 per Table 4; 5,000 sampled for finetuning across 6 eval languages
datasets.split: 5,000 random samples across the 6 evaluated languages
datasets.preprocessing: Table 6: before code <=50,000 chars, after code non-empty and different, no '#', extension check, filename not in message, message 10-1000 chars and 5-1000 words, uppercase start, 50-768 StarCoder tokens for before+special+after, message must start with an allowed imperative verb (Table 7), noise strings and regexes removed, 90% of Bump/Set version/Update version dropped; reduces dataset ~1000x. No HumanEval contamination found.

datasets.name: xP3x code subset
datasets.source: Muennighoff et al. 2022b; APPS, CodeContests, Jupyter Code Pairs, MBPP, XLCoST, Code Complex, Docstring Corpus, Great Code, State Changes; NeuralCodeSearch excluded

datasets.name: StarCoder Self-Instruct
datasets.source: Self-Instruct method with StarCoder as generator

datasets.name: OASST (filtered)
datasets.source: filtered variant from Dettmers et al. 2023 (QLoRA), plus filter removing refusals/moralizing answers
datasets.preprocessing: code fraction counted by fenced-language markers, so likely underestimated

datasets.name: HUMANEVALPACK
datasets.size: 164 problems x 6 languages x 3 tasks; 984 bugs for HumanEvalFix
datasets.source: human-written extension of HumanEval; bugs added manually by one author

models.name: SantaCoderPack
models.architecture: SantaCoder architecture with MQA, no FIM

models.name: WizardCoder, InstructCodeT5+, StarChat-beta, BLOOMZ, GPT-4, Diff Codegen 2B

training.objective: instruction tuning, loss over full sequence (masking input loss was an ablation)
training.optimizer: inferred: not stated for finetuning; SantaCoderPack pretraining uses Adam b1=0.9, b2=0.95, eps=1e-8
training.warmup: linear warmup (length not stated) for finetuning; 2% of steps for SantaCoderPack
training.tokens: 2.2 million finetuning tokens (OctoCoder); 131B tokens for SantaCoderPack (35B data repeated ~4 times)
training.regularisation: LoRA used for StarCoder finetuning (no significant difference from full finetuning observed); rank/alpha not stated
training.hardware: 32 A100 GPUs (SantaCoderPack); finetuning hardware not stated

other.hyperparameter_selection: final OctoGeeX uses the manual 1,178-sample selection; OctoCoder uses random selection

inference.samples: n = 20 samples per problem for pass@1; n = 1 for GPT-4
inference.prompting: Zero-shot. Each model uses its authors' prompt format or a simple intuitive one (Appendix Q, Figures 18-25); prompts not optimised. HumanEvalExplain caps explanation length at the docstring character count.

other.gpt4_n1_check: n=1 vs n=20 changed GPT-4 HumanEvalSynthesize Python from 75.0% to 75.2%

metrics.name: pass@1
metrics.definition: likelihood that the model solves a problem in a single attempt; estimated from n=20 samples at T=0.2, top_p=0.95; a problem is solved if generated code passes every test

metrics.name: HumanEvalExplain pass@1
metrics.definition: model explains the function under a character limit, then the same model regenerates code from its own explanation; solution overlap >=20 chars removed from the explanation; scored by execution

eval.protocol: Zero-shot pass@1 on HumanEvalPack, 3 tasks x 6 languages; execution-based; single run, no seeds or confidence intervals stated.

evidence.where: Table 2 HumanEvalSynthesize Python rows StarCoder 33.6 and OctoCoder 46.2; Table 12 row Without instruction tuning Synthesize 33.6

evidence.quote: OCTOCODER was trained for 35 steps with a sequence length of 2048 and packing corresponding to 2.2 million total finetuning tokens.

results.claim: OctoCoder reaches 46.2% pass@1 on Python HumanEvalSynthesize (the original HumanEval task), up from 33.6% for its base StarCoder, a relative 38% gain.
results.setup: StarCoder 16B instruction-tuned with LoRA on 5,000 COMMITPACKFT samples mixed with 8,587-sample filtered OASST (no OpenAI outputs); zero-shot, HumanEvalPack Python split, Synthesize task.
results.quote: With a pass@1 of 46.2% on the original Python split, OCTOCODER improves by a relative 38% over its base model, StarCoder.
results.note: The 46.2 comes from a COMMITPACKFT+OASST mix, not commit data alone. The 33.6 baseline is the pretrained StarCoder (Table 2 and Table 12 'Without instruction tuning'). Abstract says state-of-the-art among models not trained on OpenAI outputs.

results.claim: On Python HumanEvalSynthesize the commit data gives no edge over other instruction sets: OASST alone scores 46.4, Self-Instruct+OASST 46.2 and COMMITPACKFT+OASST 46.2.
results.setup: StarCoder 16B finetuned on each dataset combination (about 5,000 samples per source), Python split of HumanEvalPack.
results.table: Table 12, rows OASST (46.4), SI + OASST (46.2), COMMITPACKFT + OASST (46.2), column Synthesize
results.note: Text: 'All instruction datasets provide similar boosts for code synthesis (HUMANEVALSYNTHESIZE)'. Commits help on Fix (30.4 vs 23.1 for OASST) and the average (37.2 vs 34.7), not on Synthesize.

results.claim: COMMITPACKFT+OASST gives the best average over fix, explain and synthesize on the Python split, an absolute 23% above the no-tuning StarCoder.
results.setup: StarCoder 16B, Python split of HumanEvalPack, six data mixtures plus ablations.
results.table: Table 12, row COMMITPACKFT + OASST, column Average; row Without instruction tuning
results.note: Text says 'absolute 23% improvement'; 37.2 - 14.1 = 23.1. COMMITPACKFT + SI + xP3x + OASST is close at 37.1.

results.claim: On HumanEvalFix Python, COMMITPACKFT+OASST scores 30.4 versus 23.1 for OASST alone and 8.7 for untuned StarCoder, which the authors attribute to about 20% bug-fix commits.
results.quote: This is likely due to COMMITPACKFT including around 20% of bug fixes among other code-related tasks (Figure 2).
results.table: Table 12, rows COMMITPACKFT + OASST and OASST, column Fix
results.note: Causal explanation is a hypothesis ('likely'), not tested. Figure 2 reports Bug Fixes 19.02% of GPT-4-classified Python commits.

results.claim: OctoCoder has the highest HumanEvalPack average among permissive models; HumanEvalSynthesize average 35.5 (StarCoder 27.6), HumanEvalFix average 27.0 (StarCoder 13.4), HumanEvalExplain average 24.5.
results.setup: Zero-shot, six languages, Synthesize task; permissive models; GPT-4 scores 78.3 on the same task.
results.table: Table 2, rows OCTOCODER and StarCoder, HUMANEVALSYNTHESIZE column Avg.

results.claim: GPT-4 scores 86.6% on Python HumanEvalSynthesize but only 47.0% on HumanEvalFix and 64.6% on HumanEvalExplain Python, showing the new tasks are harder.
results.setup: GPT-4 via API, zero-shot, n=1 sample, T=0.2.
results.quote: With a pass rate of 86.6% for a single solution, GPT-4 is close to fully saturating the Python subset.
results.note: GPT-4 was earlier reported 67% (OpenAI 2023) and 81% (Bubeck et al. 2023); authors suspect API changes, contamination, or prompting.

results.claim: Instruction tuning generalises to languages unseen at tuning time (BLOOMZ on Go and Rust is above the random baseline of 0.0).
results.table: Table 2, row BLOOMZ under HUMANEVALFIX, column Go

results.claim: Python, Java and JavaScript make up about 30% of StarCoder pretraining data, Rust 1.2%; OctoCoder is best on the former and weakest on Rust.
results.quote: OCTOCODER performs weakest on Rust, which is the lowest resource language of StarCoder among the languages we benchmark (1.2% of pretraining data).

results.claim: Prompting StarCoder in the pretraining commit format scores higher on HumanEvalFix than OctoCoder: Python 32.7 vs 30.4, average 30.5 vs 27.0.
results.setup: StarCoder (which saw COMMITPACK in the format <commit_before>...<commit_msg>...<commit_after> in pretraining), zero-shot, six languages average; OctoCoder from Table 2.
results.table: Table 10, row StarCoder Commit Format, column Avg.
results.note: The format does not work for HumanEvalExplain.

results.claim: Finetuning SantaCoder on line-diff format raises HumanEvalFix Python from 7.1 to 9.9 versus commit-format finetuning at 3.8.
results.setup: SantaCoder 1.1B finetuned on Python/Java/JavaScript COMMITPACKFT with line-diff format, up to 200,000 steps, batch 64.
results.table: Table 13, row SantaCoder + Line diff format finetuning, column Python
results.note: Line diff cuts diff characters by 70% vs unified diff; does not handle insertions well.

results.claim: Models struggle most with HumanEvalFix bugs needing excess logic removed (WizardCoder solves 11.0%).
results.metric: pass@1 HumanEvalFix Python by bug type
results.setup: 164 Python bugs, 31 of them excess logic; WizardCoder.
results.table: Table 16, row Excess logic, column WizardCoder

results.claim: Filtering COMMITPACK to COMMITPACKFT shrinks it about 1000x and raises the relative change between pre- and post-commit code from 0.7% to 31%.
results.setup: Word statistics before and after the COMMITPACKFT filters.
results.quote: The percentage of code changed between pre- and post-commit is 77.6/59.1 = 1.31 (a 31% increase) as opposed to 3269.8/3269.9 = 1.007 (a 0.7% increase).

limits: The headline 46.2 vs 33.6 is HumanEvalSynthesize Python for a COMMITPACKFT+OASST mix; OASST alone scored 46.4 (Table 12), so commits are not shown to help plain synthesis. Their measured advantage is on HumanEvalFix and the average.
Single run per configuration, no seeds or confidence intervals; ablations use only the Python split and about 5,000 samples per source.
HumanEvalPack derives from HumanEval, so GPT-4 and other models may be contaminated; authors say results should be interpreted carefully.
Prompts not optimised; models without a canonical prompt (BLOOMZ, GPT-4) may be at a slight disadvantage.
Execution-based pass@k reflects functional correctness only, not code quality; LLM-based judges may be biased.
Multi-file commits filtered out; commit data only up to 2016; line-diff format does not handle insertions and is useless for explain/synthesize.
Models fail at output-length adherence in HumanEvalExplain.
GPT-4 score is far above prior reports (67%, 81%), possibly from API changes or contamination.
Classification of commit types uses GPT-4 (only for analysis in Figure 2, not for training data); LoRA rank and optimizer for finetuning not stated.
Authors suggest commit data could train reward models (code after a commit is preferred) but do not test it.
